subjects.name: Julius Caesar
clues: As a young man he was captured by pirates and later had them hunted down.
He conquered Gaul in a long campaign and wrote his own account of the wars.
In 49 BCE he led his army across the Rubicon, starting a civil war.
He formed a close alliance with Cleopatra, the queen of Egypt.
Roman leader killed by a group of senators on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.
subjects.fact: The month of July is named in his honour.

subjects.name: Cleopatra
clues: She was the last active ruler of a dynasty founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals.
Unlike earlier rulers of her family, she learned to speak the Egyptian language.
She ruled from the great port city of Alexandria and allied herself with powerful Romans.
She had children with Julius Caesar and later with Mark Antony.
The last queen of ancient Egypt, said to have died from the bite of an asp in 30 BCE.
subjects.fact: She lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

subjects.name: Alexander the Great
clues: As a boy he was taught by the philosopher Aristotle.
He tamed a famous horse called Bucephalus and rode it into many battles.
He became king at 20 after his father, Philip II, was assassinated.
His empire stretched from Greece to Egypt and on to the edge of India.
Never defeated in battle, he founded many cities named after himself and died at 32.
subjects.fact: Alexandria, one of the cities he founded, is still Egypt's second-largest city.

subjects.name: Genghis Khan
clues: Born with the name Temujin, he grew up in hardship on the open steppe.
In 1206 a great gathering of tribes proclaimed him their supreme ruler.
He set up a relay of horse riders to carry messages quickly across his lands.
He founded what became the largest connected land empire in history.
Founder of the Mongol Empire, he united the nomadic tribes of Mongolia.
subjects.fact: Mongolia's main international airport is named after him.

subjects.name: Napoleon
clues: He was born on Corsica in 1769, just a year after the island passed to French control.
He rose from artillery officer to general during a time of revolution.
He crowned himself emperor in Notre-Dame Cathedral in 1804.
His legal code still forms the basis of civil law in many countries.
This French emperor met his final defeat at Waterloo in 1815.
subjects.fact: He was about average height for his time; the 'short' myth comes partly from French and English inches differing.

subjects.name: Charlemagne
clues: This king of the Franks spent much of his long reign at war, expanding his realm.
He made Aachen his favourite home and built a grand chapel there.
His court encouraged learning, and scribes developed a clear new style of handwriting.
He united much of Western Europe, including lands that are now France and Germany.
Medieval ruler called the 'Father of Europe', crowned emperor by the Pope on Christmas Day 800.
subjects.fact: The king of hearts in a traditional French deck of cards is named after him.

subjects.name: Qin Shi Huang
clues: He became king of his state at about 13 and later conquered all its rivals.
He standardised writing, coins, weights and even the width of cart axles.
He linked earlier border walls into an early version of a famous great wall.
An army of thousands of life-size clay soldiers was buried near his tomb.
In 221 BCE he became the first emperor of a unified China.

links.name: Terracotta Army
links.rel: is guarded in death by the

subjects.fact: His clay army was found by farmers digging a well in 1974.

subjects.name: Tutankhamun
clues: He became a pharaoh at about nine years old and died before he turned twenty.
During his reign Egypt returned to its traditional gods after his father's religious changes.
His tomb in the Valley of the Kings lay almost untouched for over 3,000 years.
Howard Carter uncovered his treasure-packed tomb in 1922.
The boy pharaoh famous for his solid gold burial mask.
subjects.fact: His gold mask weighs about 10 kilograms.

subjects.name: Queen Victoria
clues: She came to the throne at just 18 after the death of her uncle, King William IV.
She married her cousin Prince Albert, and they had nine children.
Her children married into so many royal families that she was called the grandmother of Europe.
She was the first British monarch to live in Buckingham Palace.
British queen who reigned for 63 years and gave her name to a whole era.
subjects.fact: She wore white at her 1840 wedding, helping make white wedding dresses popular.

subjects.name: Elizabeth I
clues: Her father was a king who married six times.
She never married, and the American colony of Virginia was named in her honour.
During her reign William Shakespeare began writing his plays.
Her navy defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588.
The last Tudor monarch of England, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn.
subjects.fact: She reigned for 44 years, from 1558 to 1603.

subjects.name: Elizabeth II
clues: During the Second World War she trained as a driver and mechanic.
She became queen in 1952 while on a royal visit to Kenya.
Her 1953 coronation was watched live on television by millions.
She was famously fond of corgis, owning more than 30 during her life.
The longest-reigning British monarch, on the throne for 70 years until 2022.
subjects.fact: She sent her first email in 1976, from an army research base.

subjects.name: Henry VIII
clues: He was not born to be king; he became heir only after his older brother Arthur died.
A keen athlete in his youth, he loved jousting, hunting and real tennis.
He broke with the Pope in Rome and made himself head of the Church of England.
He built up the navy, and his warship the Mary Rose can be seen in a museum today.
Tudor king of England famous for having six wives.
subjects.fact: A rhyme recalls the fates of his wives: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived.

subjects.name: Marie Antoinette
clues: Born in Vienna, she was a daughter of a powerful Habsburg empress.
At 14 she was wed to the heir to the French throne.
She had a pretend farm village built in the grounds of Versailles.
She is wrongly credited with saying 'Let them eat cake'.
Queen of France and wife of Louis XVI, she lost her life during the French Revolution.
subjects.fact: The 'Let them eat cake' story appears in a book by Rousseau written when she was still a child.

subjects.name: Louis XIV
clues: He became king at the age of four.
He loved ballet and danced on stage himself as a young man.
He turned his father's hunting lodge into a vast palace with a Hall of Mirrors.
His reign of 72 years is the longest of any monarch in European history.
French king known as the Sun King, who ruled from Versailles.
subjects.fact: He is said to have declared 'I am the state', though historians doubt he ever said it.

subjects.name: George Washington
clues: As a young man he worked as a land surveyor in Virginia.
He led the Continental Army through the American Revolutionary War.
He presided over the convention that wrote the US Constitution in 1787.
He chose to step down after two terms, setting a long-lasting example.
The first President of the United States, whose face is on the one-dollar bill.

links.name: United States
links.rel: was the first president of the

subjects.fact: He never lived in the White House; it was finished after his presidency.

subjects.name: Abraham Lincoln
clues: Largely self-taught, he was born in a log cabin in Kentucky.
He worked as a lawyer in Illinois before entering national politics.
At 6 feet 4 inches, he was the tallest US president.
His short Gettysburg Address in 1863 is one of the most famous speeches ever.
16th US president, who led the Union through the Civil War and issued the Emancipation Proclamation.

links.name: Battle of Gettysburg
links.rel: gave a famous address at the site of the

subjects.fact: He is the only US president to have held a patent, for a device to lift boats over shallow water.

subjects.name: Winston Churchill
clues: As a young war reporter he escaped from a prisoner-of-war camp in South Africa.
He was a keen painter and produced over 500 canvases.
He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.
He offered 'blood, toil, tears and sweat' in his first speech as wartime leader.
British prime minister who led the country through most of the Second World War.
subjects.fact: His mother, Jennie Jerome, was born in the United States.

subjects.name: Nelson Mandela
clues: He trained as a lawyer and opened a law firm in Johannesburg with a friend.
He spent 27 years in prison, many of them on Robben Island.
After his release in 1990 he worked to end apartheid peacefully.
He shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk.
South Africa's first Black president, elected in 1994.
subjects.fact: His birthday, 18 July, is marked by the United Nations as an international day of service.

subjects.name: John F. Kennedy
clues: During the Second World War he commanded a small patrol boat in the Pacific.
His book Profiles in Courage won a Pulitzer Prize.
In 1961 he set the goal of landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out.
At 43, he was the youngest person ever elected US president.
35th US president, assassinated in Dallas in November 1963.
subjects.fact: He was the first US president born in the 20th century.

subjects.name: Simón Bolívar
clues: Born in Caracas, he was orphaned as a child and partly educated in Europe.
As a young man he vowed in Rome to free his homeland from Spanish rule.
He led his armies across the high Andes in a daring campaign in 1819.
He helped win independence for what are now Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Panama.
Known as 'The Liberator', he has a South American country named after him.
subjects.fact: Venezuela's currency, the bolívar, is also named after him.

subjects.name: Joan of Arc
clues: A peasant girl, she said she heard voices urging her to save her country.
At about 17 she helped lift the siege of Orléans in 1429.
She saw the French king Charles VII crowned at Reims.
She was captured by her enemies and put to death in 1431, aged about 19.
French heroine of the Hundred Years' War, later declared a saint.
subjects.fact: She is one of the patron saints of France.

subjects.name: Mahatma Gandhi
clues: He studied law in London and then worked for about 21 years in South Africa.
He spun his own cloth on a spinning wheel to promote homemade goods.
In 1930 he led a 24-day march to the sea to protest a tax on salt.
His non-violent resistance inspired Martin Luther King Jr.
Leader of India's independence movement, honoured as the Father of the Nation.
subjects.fact: His birthday, 2 October, is marked worldwide as the International Day of Non-Violence.

subjects.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
clues: The son of a pastor, he became a Baptist minister in Montgomery, Alabama.
He led the Montgomery bus boycott after Rosa Parks' arrest in 1955.
At 35 he became the youngest man then to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
He gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech at the Lincoln Memorial in 1963.
American civil rights leader honoured with a US national holiday each January.

links.name: United States
links.rel: led the civil rights movement in the

subjects.fact: He was first named Michael; his father later changed both their names to honour Martin Luther.

subjects.name: Rosa Parks
clues: Born in Tuskegee, Alabama, she later worked as a seamstress.
She served as secretary of her local branch of the NAACP.
In December 1955 she refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery.
Her arrest sparked a bus boycott that lasted more than a year.
Civil rights pioneer called 'the mother of the freedom movement'.

links.name: United States
links.rel: campaigned for civil rights in the

subjects.fact: The bus she rode is now displayed at the Henry Ford Museum in Michigan.

subjects.name: Harriet Tubman
clues: Born into slavery in Maryland, she escaped to freedom in 1849.
She went back south about 13 times to guide others to freedom.
She was a 'conductor' on the Underground Railroad, a secret network of safe houses.
During the Civil War she served as a scout and spy for the Union army.
Abolitionist nicknamed 'Moses' who said she never lost a passenger.
subjects.fact: She guided a raid at Combahee Ferry in 1863 that freed more than 700 people.

subjects.name: Emmeline Pankhurst
clues: Born in Manchester, she founded a women's political group there in 1903.
Her group's motto was 'Deeds, not words'.
She was imprisoned many times and went on hunger strikes.
Her daughters Christabel and Sylvia also campaigned alongside her.
British suffragette leader who fought for women's right to vote.

links.name: United Kingdom
links.rel: campaigned for votes for women in the

subjects.fact: British women won equal voting rights with men in 1928, just weeks after her death.

subjects.name: Christopher Columbus
clues: Born in the port city of Genoa, he became a skilled sailor.
He spent years asking European courts to pay for a voyage west to reach Asia.
Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain finally backed his expedition.
His three ships were the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María.
Explorer who crossed the Atlantic and reached the Americas in 1492.

links.name: Italy
links.rel: was born in what is now

subjects.fact: He made four voyages across the Atlantic but believed to the end that he had reached Asia.

subjects.name: Marco Polo
clues: He set out from Venice as a teenager with his father and uncle.
He spent about 17 years in the service of the ruler Kublai Khan.
He returned home after about 24 years away.
While held prisoner in Genoa, he told his stories to a writer of romances.
Venetian merchant famous for his book of travels to China.
subjects.fact: A popular swimming-pool game of tag is named after him.

subjects.name: Ferdinand Magellan
clues: This Portuguese-born sailor led an expedition for the Spanish crown.
In 1519 he set out with five ships to find a western route to the Spice Islands.
He found a passage at the tip of South America that now bears his name.
He named the Pacific Ocean for its calm waters.
His expedition made the first voyage around the world, though he died on the way.
subjects.fact: Only one of his five ships, the Victoria, completed the voyage, with 18 survivors.

subjects.name: Vasco da Gama
clues: He sailed from Lisbon in 1497 with four ships.
He rounded the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa.
He reached Calicut on the coast of India in 1498.
His voyage opened a sea route for the spice trade between Europe and Asia.
Portuguese explorer who was the first European to reach India by sea.
subjects.fact: He returned to India later in life and died there in 1524.

subjects.name: Roald Amundsen
clues: He was the first to sail the whole Northwest Passage, a trip that took three years.
He learned cold-weather survival skills from the Inuit.
His team relied on dog sleds and skis on their most famous expedition.
In 1911 he beat Robert Falcon Scott in a race to the South Pole.
Norwegian explorer who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole.
subjects.fact: He also flew over the North Pole in an airship in 1926.

subjects.name: James Cook
clues: He began his working life on coal-carrying ships out of Whitby.
His accurate charts of Newfoundland impressed the Royal Navy.
He led three great voyages across the Pacific Ocean in the 1700s.
In 1770 his ship Endeavour reached the east coast of Australia.
British navigator who mapped New Zealand and Australia's east coast.
subjects.fact: He helped prevent scurvy on his voyages by feeding his crew sauerkraut.

subjects.name: Edmund Hillary
clues: He worked as a beekeeper in New Zealand before becoming famous.
He served as a navigator in the air force during the Second World War.
In 1958 he drove farm tractors all the way to the South Pole.
He later built schools and hospitals for Sherpa communities in Nepal.
With Tenzing Norgay, he made the first confirmed climb to the top of Mount Everest.
subjects.fact: His face appears on New Zealand's five-dollar note.

subjects.name: French Revolution
clues: It began in 1789 after the king called a meeting of the Estates-General.
A crowd stormed a Paris fortress-prison on 14 July.
Its rallying cry was 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity'.
It brought in the metric system and swept away the monarchy.
The upheaval in France that led to the downfall of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette.
subjects.fact: France's national day, 14 July, marks the storming of the Bastille.

subjects.name: Fall of the Berlin Wall
clues: It happened after a government spokesman mistakenly announced new travel rules.
Crowds gathered at the checkpoints until the guards finally opened the gates.
People chipped at the concrete with hammers and kept pieces as souvenirs.
The barrier had divided a German city for 28 years.
The night of 9 November 1989, when East Germans crossed freely to the West.
subjects.fact: Germany was formally reunified less than a year later, on 3 October 1990.

subjects.name: RMS Titanic
clues: It was built in Belfast at the Harland and Wolff shipyard.
It set sail from Southampton in April 1912, bound for New York.
It did not carry enough lifeboats for everyone on board.
It struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic on its first voyage.
The 'unsinkable' ocean liner that sank in 1912.
subjects.fact: Its wreck was found in 1985, about 3,800 metres below the surface.

subjects.name: Magna Carta
clues: It was sealed in June 1215 in a meadow beside the River Thames.
Rebel barons forced an unpopular king to agree to it.
King John accepted it, but the Pope cancelled it within months.
It set out the idea that even the king had to obey the law.
England's 'Great Charter', a founding text of rights and liberty.
subjects.fact: Four original copies from 1215 still survive.

subjects.name: Boston Tea Party
clues: It took place on a cold December night in 1773.
Protesters, some disguised as Mohawk people, boarded three ships.
They dumped 342 chests of tea into the harbour.
It was a protest against taxes set by the British government without colonists' votes.
Famous protest in a Massachusetts harbour that helped spark the American Revolution.

links.name: United States
links.rel: helped lead to the founding of the

subjects.fact: The tea belonged to the British East India Company.

subjects.name: Great Fire of London
clues: It started in a bakery on Pudding Lane in September 1666.
It burned for about four days and destroyed over 13,000 houses.
The diarist Samuel Pepys buried his parmesan cheese to save it.
Old St Paul's Cathedral was destroyed and later rebuilt by Christopher Wren.
The blaze of 1666 that destroyed much of England's capital.
subjects.fact: A 61-metre column called the Monument stands near where it began.

subjects.name: Industrial Revolution
clues: It began in Britain in the second half of the 18th century.
Steam engines improved by James Watt powered mills and mines.
Cotton spinning moved out of homes and into large factories.
Railways and canals spread to carry coal and goods.
The era when machines and factories transformed how goods were made.

links.name: James Watt
links.rel: was powered by the engines of

subjects.fact: The world's first public steam railway, the Stockton and Darlington, opened in 1825.

subjects.name: Fall of Constantinople
clues: It ended in May 1453 after a siege of about 53 days.
The attackers used giant cannons to pound the city's ancient walls.
Ships were dragged overland to get around a chain across the Golden Horn.
Sultan Mehmed II was just 21 years old when he led the attack.
The capture of the Byzantine capital by the Ottoman Turks.

links.name: Istanbul
links.rel: took place in what is now

links.name: Turkey
links.rel: is a key moment in the history of

subjects.fact: The city later became known as Istanbul.

subjects.name: California Gold Rush
clues: It began when a carpenter spotted shiny flakes at Sutter's Mill in January 1848.
About 300,000 people arrived hoping to strike it rich.
Fortune seekers who arrived in 1849 were nicknamed 'forty-niners'.
San Francisco grew from a small settlement into a boom town.
The great hunt for gold in the American West that began in 1848.
subjects.fact: San Francisco's American football team, the 49ers, is named after the gold seekers.

subjects.name: Declaration of Independence
clues: It was mostly drafted by Thomas Jefferson in a few weeks.
The Continental Congress adopted it in Philadelphia.
John Hancock's large signature on it became famous.
It says all men are created equal, with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
The document of 4 July 1776 announcing the 13 colonies' break from Britain.
subjects.fact: Thomas Jefferson and John Adams both died on its 50th anniversary, 4 July 1826.

subjects.name: World War I
clues: It began in 1914 after the assassination of an archduke in Sarajevo.
Much of it was fought from long lines of muddy trenches.
Tanks were used in battle for the first time during it.
An unofficial Christmas truce in 1914 saw soldiers meet and play football.
The global conflict of 1914 to 1918 that ended with an armistice on 11 November.
subjects.fact: Many countries still mark 11 November, the day the fighting stopped.

subjects.name: World War II
clues: It began in Europe in September 1939 with the invasion of Poland.
Codebreakers at Bletchley Park cracked secret Enigma messages.
Britain's Winston Churchill was a key Allied leader.
The D-Day landings in 1944 opened a new front in Western Europe.
The global conflict of 1939 to 1945, the largest war in history.
subjects.fact: It ended in Europe on 8 May 1945, celebrated as VE Day.

subjects.name: American Civil War
clues: It began in 1861 when Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter.
Eleven southern states tried to break away and form their own nation.
Generals Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee led opposing armies.
It ended in 1865 with Lee's surrender at Appomattox.
The war between the Union and the Confederacy in the United States.

links.name: Abraham Lincoln
links.rel: was led on the Union side by

subjects.fact: It led to the end of slavery in the US through the 13th Amendment in 1865.

subjects.name: Hundred Years' War
clues: It began when an English king claimed the right to rule a neighbouring kingdom.
It ran from 1337 to 1453, with long spells of peace in between.
English longbowmen won famous victories at Crécy and Agincourt.
Joan of Arc helped turn the tide for France.
The long medieval struggle between England and France over the French crown.
subjects.fact: Despite its name, it lasted 116 years.

subjects.name: Battle of Hastings
clues: It was fought on 14 October 1066 on a ridge in Sussex.
The defenders had marched south just after beating a Viking army in the north.
The Bayeux Tapestry tells its story in embroidered pictures.
King Harold II was killed, traditionally by an arrow in the eye.
The victory that made William the Conqueror king of England.
subjects.fact: The nearby town is simply called Battle, after the fight.

subjects.name: Battle of Waterloo
clues: It was fought on 18 June 1815 near a village south of Brussels.
The Duke of Wellington led an allied army against the French.
Prussian troops under Blücher arrived in time to help win the day.
It ended the Hundred Days, an emperor's brief return to power.
Napoleon's final defeat, in what is now Belgium.

links.name: Belgium
links.rel: was fought in what is now

subjects.fact: To 'meet your Waterloo' has come to mean facing a final defeat.

subjects.name: Battle of Gettysburg
clues: It was fought over three days in early July 1863.
It took place around a small town in Pennsylvania.
Pickett's Charge on the last day failed against Union lines.
It is often called the turning point of the war.
Civil War battle whose site Lincoln honoured with a famous short address.

links.name: American Civil War
links.rel: was a turning point of the

links.name: Abraham Lincoln
links.rel: was honoured in a speech by

subjects.fact: Lincoln's address there was about 270 words long and took around two minutes.

subjects.name: D-Day
clues: It was postponed by a day because of stormy weather.
Allied planners used fake armies and dummy paratroopers to fool the enemy.
Its beaches were code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword.
About 156,000 troops crossed the English Channel on the first day.
The Allied invasion of northern France on 6 June 1944.
subjects.fact: It remains the largest seaborne invasion in history.

subjects.name: Battle of Thermopylae
clues: It was fought in 480 BCE at a narrow coastal pass.
A small Greek force held off a huge Persian army for three days.
The Persian king Xerxes led the invading force.
King Leonidas and his 300 Spartans made a famous last stand.
The ancient battle at the 'Hot Gates' that inspired the story of the 300.
subjects.fact: A local man showed the Persians a mountain path around the Greek position.
